content: The use of pyrethroid-only insecticide-treated nets (ITNs) or curtains likely reduces the incidence of severe malaria episodes compared to untreated nets or curtains. This conclusion is based on evidence from 23 studies, including 21 cluster randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and 2 individual RCTs. Among these, 12 studies compared ITNs with untreated nets, while 11 studies compared ITNs with no nets. The studies were conducted across various regions: 12 in Africa (including Burkina Faso, Côte d’Ivoire, Cameroon, Gambia, Ghana, Kenya, Madagascar, Sierra Leone, and Tanzania), 6 in the Americas (Colombia, Ecuador, Nicaragua, Peru, and Venezuela), 4 in South-East Asia (India, Myanmar, and Thailand), and 1 in the Eastern Mediterranean (Pakistan). Pyrethroid-only ITNs or curtains probably reduce all-cause child mortality compared to untreated nets or curtains, with moderate certainty evidence. They also reduce the incidence of uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria episodes compared to untreated nets or curtains, supported by high-certainty evidence. Additionally, pyrethroid-only ITNs or curtains reduce the prevalence of P. falciparum malaria compared to untreated nets or curtains, with high-certainty evidence. However, their effect on the incidence of uncomplicated P. vivax malaria episodes is less certain, with low-certainty evidence. The evidence regarding their impact on P. vivax prevalence is very uncertain, with very low-certainty evidence. In areas with high insecticide resistance, ITNs treated with both piperonyl butoxide (PBO) and pyrethroid were found to reduce malaria parasite prevalence at 4-6 months follow-up compared to pyrethroid-only ITNs, based on high-certainty evidence from two cluster RCTs conducted in Uganda and Tanzania. At 9-12 months follow-up, PBO-pyrethroid ITNs probably reduce malaria parasite prevalence compared to pyrethroid-only ITNs, with moderate-certainty evidence. Similar reductions were observed at 16-18 months and 21-25 months follow-up, although the certainty of evidence was moderate due to serious inconsistency. Experimental hut trials conducted in Benin, Burkina Faso, Cameroon, Côte d’Ivoire, and Tanzania demonstrated that unwashed PBO-pyrethroid ITNs result in lower mosquito blood-feeding success compared to unwashed pyrethroid-only ITNs. Similarly, washed PBO-pyrethroid ITNs showed reduced mosquito blood-feeding success compared to washed pyrethroid-only ITNs. In areas of high malaria transmission and pyrethroid resistance, ITNs treated with pyrethroid-chlorfenapyr (a dual-active ingredient) were compared to pyrethroid-only ITNs in two RCTs conducted in Benin and Tanzania. These trials demonstrated that pyrethroid-chlorfenapyr ITNs are more effective in reducing malaria transmission. However, the evidence is limited by serious imprecision and inconsistency in some outcomes. Overall, the findings support the use of ITNs with dual-active ingredients, such as PBO-pyrethroid or pyrethroid-chlorfenapyr, in areas with high insecticide resistance to enhance malaria control efforts.
